column5: endless smoke; no rest day or night
column6: The commentary reads the continuing state in the fire as unrelieved, even without sleep or rest; Revelation says the beast-worshipers have no rest day or night and the smoke of their torment rises forever, giving a close image of conscious, unending punishment.

column5: torment day and night forever
column6: The commentary stresses that the person remains in the fire without death or release; Revelation depicts the devil, beast, and false prophet tormented day and night forever, a direct parallel for punishment whose duration has no end.

column5: lake of fire called second death
column6: The commentary says the condemned person in the fire does not die; Revelation calls the lake of fire “the second death,” an explicit counter-description of the same final-fire image.

column5: Peshitta cognates of Arabic ḥ-y-y and m-w-t
column6: The commentary explicitly negates its Arabic verbs yahyā (“lives”) and yamūtu (“dies”); the Syriac Peshitta at this verse uses cognate life and death roots in Jesus’ promise that the one who lives and believes will never die, giving an opposite destiny in the same paired terms.

column5: Hebrew ḥ-y-h and m-w-t; choosing life
column6: The commentary’s Arabic yahyā and yamūtu mean “lives” and “dies”; Deuteronomy uses their Hebrew cognates for life and death when Moses sets the two before Israel and commands them to choose life, adding a covenantal choice to the commentary’s warning that preferring near life ends in neither life nor death.

column5: twelve-month Gehinnom; consumed and scattered
column6: The commentary presents the fire as a state in which death never comes; this Mishnah says the wicked are judged in Gehinnom for twelve months and then their bodies are consumed, their souls burned, and their ashes scattered, a finite and terminal account of punishment.

column5: fire and sulfur; torment before the Lamb
column6: The commentary identifies fīhā as the great fire in which the condemned remain; Revelation’s preceding verse depicts the beast-worshipers tormented with fire and sulfur, a specific shared image of final punishment.

column5: corpses; worm does not die; fire not quenched
column6: The commentary says the person in the fire neither dies nor lives; Isaiah’s closing vision shows the corpses of rebels while their worm does not die and their fire is not quenched, sharing unending punishment imagery while locating endurance in the worm and fire rather than in living human victims.

column5: Isaiah’s undying worm applied to Gehenna
column6: The commentary describes an ongoing state in the fire; Jesus invokes Isaiah’s undying worm and unquenched fire as Gehenna’s warning, carrying Isaiah’s judgment image into a teaching about a person’s final fate without saying that the person cannot die.

column5: conscious anguish in flame; denied water
column6: The commentary says the damned retain the capacity to feel pain and cannot find relief; in the parable the dead rich man is in anguish in flame and asks for water to cool his tongue, a concrete scene of postmortem sensation.

column5: fixed gulf bars passage
column6: The commentary repeatedly closes the possibility of leaving the place of punishment; Abraham says a great chasm prevents passage between the rich man’s place of torment and the place of comfort, a specific barrier though it separates abodes rather than describing an exit from Hades.

column5: the dead rich man conscious in Hades
column6: The commentary describes the condemned person’s continuing condition after entering the fire; Luke’s rich man is already dead yet conscious and tormented in Hades, offering a distinct Christian picture of postmortem awareness.

column5: sleepers awaken to two outcomes
column6: The commentary insists that the person in the fire is neither dead nor alive; Daniel depicts sleepers in the dust awakening, some to everlasting life and others to disgrace, a Jewish apocalyptic alternative in which the dead rise into one of two outcomes.

column5: resurrection of life or judgment
column6: The commentary’s double negation leaves no way out through either death or life; Jesus says the dead in the tombs will come out to resurrection of life or resurrection of judgment, a contrasting Christian account of two postmortem destinies.

column5: eternal punishment opposite eternal life
column6: The commentary places the damned in an unending state without life; Jesus’ judgment saying sends one group to eternal punishment and the righteous to eternal life, preserving the lasting divide while naming the condemned state as punishment rather than “neither life nor death.”

column5: the dead rest; turmoil ceases
column6: The commentary extends “does not die” to the denial of sleep and stillness; Job imagines Sheol as a place where the wicked cease turmoil and the weary rest, making the condemned person’s lack of deathly rest especially stark.

column5: righteous souls safe from torment
column6: The commentary’s condemned person remains in torment without dying; Wisdom says the souls of the righteous are in God’s hand and no torment touches them, a Jewish contrast between the punished and the protected dead.

column5: hope of immortality
column6: The commentary distinguishes mere endless existence from the full life of the hereafter; Wisdom says the righteous’ hope is full of immortality, a positive postmortem life sharply unlike the condemned person’s denied life.

column5: resurrection to eternal life after death
column6: The commentary says the condemned person receives neither death nor life; the martyr says the King of the world will raise the faithful to renewed eternal life after death, presenting death as a passage to life rather than a closed state.

column5: death ends amid comfort and life
column6: The commentary notes that not dying can describe both the blessed and the damned, with the absence of life making the fire different; Revelation’s new creation has no more death, but its setting is God’s consoling presence, clarifying the difference between deathlessness with life and deathlessness without it.

column5: river of the water of life
column6: The commentary develops life as growth and ties living vegetation to life-giving rain; Revelation’s final vision has a river of the water of life flowing from God’s throne, a concrete image of the full life absent from the condemned person.

column5: Zechariah’s promised son named John
column6: The commentary links ayah 87:13’s verb yahyā (“lives”) to the prophet Yahya, whose birth was announced to elderly Zechariah; Luke’s angel answers Zechariah’s prayer and names the promised son John, paralleling the birth-announcement scene while the Greek name does not carry the Arabic life-wordplay.

column5: Herod says executed John has been raised
column6: The commentary contrasts the condemned person who will not live with Yahya, whose death and being raised alive are blessed; after John’s execution Herod says he has been raised, a Christian tradition about the same prophet that turns on death and resurrection but appears only as Herod’s mistaken report.

column5: barrier to eating the tree of life
column6: The commentary recalls Adam’s descent from the garden and contrasts earthly life and death with the fire where neither occurs; Genesis says God bars access to the tree lest the human live forever, adding the Hebrew story’s distinct boundary around post-Eden life.

column5: Adam sent from Eden to work the soil
column6: The commentary uses Adam’s descent to frame the earth as a place where people live and die; Genesis sends Adam from Eden to till the ground, supplying the corresponding expulsion scene and its mortal, soil-bound setting.

column5: twelve months for some; others for generations
column6: The commentary presents the fire’s state as unending; the Talmud assigns twelve months in Gehinnom and ashes afterward to some sinners but says other classes are confined for generations, showing how rabbinic interpretation differentiates the duration of punishment.

column5: the dead know nothing
column6: The commentary’s fire preserves awareness and the ability to feel pain; Qohelet says the dead know nothing and their memory is forgotten, a contrary account of death, though its “under the sun” frame makes its relation to final judgment uncertain.

column5: accursed valley reserved for judgment
column6: The commentary treats the fire as the lasting place of the condemned; Enoch describes an accursed valley where those cursed forever are gathered for judgment, a specific apocalyptic place-of-punishment image that does not itself say they neither die nor live.

column5: seek death but cannot find it
column6: The commentary notes that the condemned plead for death yet remain in torment; during the locust plague Revelation says people seek death and it flees from them, a striking parallel to death denied as release, though the scene is earthly apocalyptic suffering rather than final hell.

column5: waiting for death that does not come
column6: The commentary describes people in the fire asking for death without receiving it; Job’s lament depicts those who wait for death, but it does not come, giving the same specific frustration in present anguish rather than afterlife punishment.

column5: destroy both body and soul in Gehenna
column6: The commentary says the person in the fire does not die; Jesus warns of the one able to destroy both body and soul in Gehenna, a potentially terminal account of the same fate, though “destroy” can also mean ruin and need not imply annihilation.

column5: YHWH kills, makes alive, raises from Sheol
column6: The commentary reads the opening “then” against the Qur’an’s usual transitions between death and life, before the final state with neither; Hannah’s hymn says YHWH puts to death and makes alive, brings down to Sheol and raises, supplying a compact formula of transitions the ayah suspends.

column5: Hebrew m-w-t and ḥ-y-h in a call to turn and live
column6: The commentary’s Arabic yamūtu and yahyā mean “dies” and “lives”; Ezekiel uses the Hebrew cognates when YHWH says he takes no pleasure in anyone’s death and calls the sinner to turn and live, setting a prophetic invitation to life beside the commentary’s consequence for refusing reminder.

column5: Wisdom will not answer the late call
column6: The commentary says the one who avoided the reminder eventually has no way out; personified Wisdom says that after hearers reject her call, she will not answer when they later call, adding the sequence from ignored warning to unavailable relief.

column5: Hebrew ḥayyîm as the result of finding Wisdom
column6: The commentary develops life as the good that comes through receiving reminder; personified Wisdom says whoever finds her finds life and favor from YHWH, using the Hebrew cognate of Arabic ḥ-y-y for life gained by heeding instruction.

column5: hating Wisdom is loving death
column6: The commentary connects avoiding the reminder with the final loss of life; Wisdom says those who hate her love death, making rejection itself a chosen death in contrast with the Qur’anic sinner’s inability to die as well as to live.

column5: fire and water set before the chooser
column6: The commentary connects preferring near life with ending in the fire; Sirach sets fire and water before a person’s hand as an ethical choice, giving a concrete meeting of choice and fire without claiming the same account of the afterlife.

column5: life and death before each person
column6: The commentary says the condemned person reaches neither of the ordinary alternatives, life or death; Sirach says life and death are set before a person and the chosen outcome is given, a Jewish wisdom formulation of moral choice that sharpens the contrast.

column5: wicked claim death ends life without return
column6: The commentary recalls deniers who say worldly life is all there is and deny resurrection; Wisdom’s wicked make the same kind of claim, calling life short and saying no one is known to have returned from Hades, after which the book contests their judgment.

column5: “enjoy good things now”
column6: The commentary says people prefer near life and leave the more lasting hereafter; Wisdom’s wicked urge one another to enjoy good things in the present, supplying a specific Jewish depiction of that preference before the text exposes its error.

column5: furnace of Gehenna opposite rest and paradise
column6: The commentary develops the fire as a place without rest and contrasts it with the blessed abode; 4 Ezra sets the furnace of Gehenna opposite paradise and the place of torment opposite rest, giving an explicit apocalyptic two-abode frame.

column5: righteous called living after death; wicked dead while alive
column6: The commentary distinguishes bodily death from moral and receptive “life”; a rabbinic maxim says the righteous are called living even after death and the wicked dead even in life, extending that secondary moral sense. The remembered citation lies in the cemetery discussion around these folios.

column5: second death has no authority over the blessed
column6: The commentary notes that not dying is common to both final abodes, while the fire is distinguished by lack of life; Revelation says the second death has no authority over those sharing the first resurrection, showing deathlessness as a blessed state with life.

column5: sin’s wage is death; God’s gift is life
column6: The commentary links refusal of reminder and preference for near life to the sinner’s final state, where neither death nor life is granted; Paul instead names death as sin’s wage and eternal life as God’s gift, a contrasting account of the outcome.

column5: lifelong slavery through fear of death
column6: The commentary presents the condemned state as worse than an execution threat because death cannot release the person; Hebrews says fear of death enslaves people throughout life and describes Christ’s release from that bondage, a different Christian treatment of death’s power.

column5: Sheol and death cannot praise or hope
column6: The commentary says the condemned neither dies nor lives after turning from reminder; Hezekiah’s prayer says Sheol cannot thank God and death cannot praise, distinguishing the dead from the living worshiper rather than describing an intermediate state.

column5: the living give thanks
column6: The commentary links life with receiving reminder and the surah’s prayerful remembrance; Hezekiah says the living, the living give thanks to God, making the loss of life also a loss of ordinary praise.

column5: dust returns to dust
column6: The commentary contrasts earthly existence, where people live and die, with the fire where neither happens; Genesis tells Adam he will return to the ground from which he was taken, specifying ordinary mortality in the Eden-to-earth frame.

column5: death preferred to life in catastrophe
column6: The commentary cites pleas for death from people who cannot escape punishment; Jeremiah says survivors of calamity will regard death as preferable to life, a specific reversal of the condemned person’s inability to receive the death he seeks.
